faq.a: Women have a wider pelvis and a larger femoral canal, predisposing to herniation.
faq.q: Why are femoral hernias more common in women?

faq.a: Yes; femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament, whereas inguinal hernias are above it.
faq.q: Can a femoral canal hernia be confused with an inguinal hernia?

faq.a: It is the solitary lymph node within the femoral canal, draining the lower limb to the external iliac nodes.

exam: A 68‑year‑old woman presents with a tender groin lump below the inguinal ligament that is non‑reducible – what is the next immediate step? — Assess for signs of strangulation and arrange urgent surgical referral.

How does the anatomy of the femoral canal explain why femoral hernias have a higher risk of strangulation than inguinal hernias? — The canal is a rigid, narrow space bounded by ligaments, limiting expansion of herniated contents.

During a groin examination you feel a pulsatile mass inferior to the inguinal ligament – what condition does this suggest and why is it important? — Femoral artery aneurysm; risk of rupture and distal ischemia.
Explain why a patient with chronic cough is predisposed to a femoral hernia. — Repeated Valsalva increases intra‑abdominal pressure, forcing abdominal contents into the femoral canal.

In a low‑resource hospital without CT, how would you differentiate a strangulated femoral hernia from a simple incarcerated one? — Look for systemic signs (fever, tachycardia), persistent pain, and inability to reduce; these indicate strangulation.

What lymphatic pathway is associated with the femoral canal and why is it clinically relevant in cancer staging? — Drainage to external iliac nodes; metastasis from lower‑limb melanomas may travel this route.
Why must a surgeon avoid excessive dissection of the lacunar ligament during femoral hernia repair? — To prevent injury to the femoral vein and preserve venous outflow.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with a painful groin mass – how might the femoral canal be involved? — Sickle cell vaso‑occlusion can cause thrombosis of the femoral vein, leading to canal distension and mimicking a hernia.
ai.title: Femoral Canal Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The femoral canal is a short medial compartment of the femoral sheath containing fat and Cloquet's node, allowing venous expansion and lymphatic drainage. Its anatomy is crucial for recognizing femoral hernias and vascular emergencies in low‑resource settings.

b: Provides space for femoral vein distension
Acts as a conduit for lymph from the lower limb to external iliac nodes
sections.p: The femoral canal is the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, about 2 cm long, lying deep to the femoral vein. It contains a small fat pad and the lymph node known as Cloquet's node.

b: Contains loose areolar tissue and Cloquet's node
sections.p: Within the femoral triangle, the sheath encloses (lateral to medial) the femoral nerve, artery, vein, and finally the canal. The canal is bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineal (Cooper's) ligament, and medially by the lacunar ligament.

b: Close to the femoral vein – important in venous thrombosis
Proximity to the femoral artery explains risk of arterial injury during hernia repair
sections.p: Medially the canal abuts the lacunar ligament; laterally it is adjacent to the femoral vein. The canal lies superficial to the femoral sheath's posterior wall and deep to the inguinal ligament.

b: Small arterial branches provide nutrition to the fat pad and Cloquet's node
sections.p: The canal itself has no major arterial supply; its walls receive small branches from the femoral artery and the profunda femoris perforators.

b: Pain from canal pathology may be referred to the upper thigh
sections.p: Sensory innervation derives from the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the iliohypogastric nerve.

b: Provides a route for metastatic spread from lower limb
sections.p: The canal permits expansion of the femoral vein during increased intra‑abdominal pressure and serves as a lymphatic pathway via Cloquet's node to the external iliac nodes.

b: Higher incidence in women due to wider pelvis
Risk increased by chronic cough, constipation, pregnancy
Strangulated femoral hernia → bowel necrosis, sepsis, death if untreated
sections.p: Femoral hernias protrude through the femoral canal, presenting as a tender, irreducible mass below the inguinal ligament. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation leads to strangulation and gangrene, a surgical emergency.
On examination, a femoral hernia is felt inferior to the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle, and may be reducible. A pulsatile mass suggests a femoral artery aneurysm, not a hernia.

t.b: Confirms hernia sac versus vascular lesion; shows bowel loops or fat in canal
Defines hernia size, signs of strangulation; guides surgical planning
When imaging unavailable, rely on history (pain, vomiting), exam (non‑reducible, tender mass), and signs of obstruction

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe groin pain with a non‑reducible mass, vomiting, or fever – suspect strangulated femoral hernia
Rapid swelling with pulsatile mass – consider femoral artery aneurysm rupture
